title: Beshalach: bitter water made sweet (Exodus 15:22–26)
hook: at Marah the water is bitter until a tree is thrown in

segments.voice: Yesterday the people stood at the sea and God said go forward. Your line was pray, then go forward. Did you take a first step? Today, still in Beshalach, they're across, and three days later, thirsty. Day three hundred forty-one.

Big wins have a strange aftertaste. The wedding is over and now there are thank-you notes. The new job starts and the commute is awful. The graduation party ends and the loans begin. The Israelites have just walked through the sea on dry land. They've sung a song that is still part of Jewish morning prayer. And three days later, in the wilderness of Shur, they still haven't found water. When they finally do, at a place called Marah, they lift it to their lips and spit it out.
screen: `THE WIN, THEN THE AFTERTASTE.` → `THREE DAYS, NO WATER.` → `MARAH: THEY SPIT IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Marah means bitter. The place is named for the water, and the people do what thirsty people do: they complain to Moses. What shall we drink? Moses cries out to God, and God shows him a tree, a piece of wood. Moses throws it into the water, and in the old Jewish translation, "the waters were made sweet." That's it. A few verses. The Torah doesn't say what kind of tree it was, and the rabbis couldn't resist asking. In the Mekhilta, an early commentary, several sages each name a different tree. One opinion is that it was itself bitter, and the lesson is that God can heal bitter with bitter. Another says the tree stands for the words of Torah, which the rabbis link to the tree of life in the book of Proverbs. And then the story ends with a line about God: "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." Notice what the story doesn't do. It doesn't scold them for being thirsty. It doesn't take them back to the sea. The bitterness is real, and something is thrown into the middle of it, and it changes. Sometimes the change is a tree in the water: a meal someone brings, a joke at the right moment, an old song, a page of something wise. Small things, dropped into the bitter part.
screen: `MARAH: BITTER.` · `A TREE THROWN IN, MADE SWEET.` · `WHICH TREE? THE SAGES DISAGREE.` · `THE LORD THAT HEALETH THEE.` · then, large: `A TREE IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the bitter water. Settle, and breathe. Think of one bitter thing in your life right now. Not the biggest one. A smaller one: a tense email thread, a chore you hate, a sour mood between you and someone. Taste it honestly. Then ask: what's one small thing I could throw into it? A kind word, a cup of tea, a walk, a sentence of thanks, a song. Picture dropping it in. If you pray, you can hold the line from Marah, the LORD that healeth thee. The bell holds the time.
Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where just past the sea the water turns bitter, and a tree thrown in makes it sweet.
Your line: a tree in the water. Today, when something tastes bitter, look for one small thing to drop into it. Day three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: The Song at the Sea, sung just before the Marah story, is part of the daily morning service, and the words of Exodus 15:26 about the LORD who heals are echoed in Jewish prayers for healing.

fork.setup: you're Moses at Marah. the people are thirsty and the water is bitter. what does God show you?
options: a new well a day's walk away.
a tree to throw into the water.
fork.reveal: a tree. Moses throws it in, and the waters are made sweet. the rock comes later, in another story.

original.note: Hebrew: bitter. the name of the place, after its water.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic stick fixed the water.
what it means: something small thrown into the bitter part changes it.
what a scholar hears: the Mekhilta records several sages naming different trees, and one reading of the tree as words of Torah.

sources.quoted: for I am the LORD that healeth thee.

notes: Exodus 15:25 and 15:26 phrases quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (KJV has the same words); verify.

Mekhilta (Vayassa 1): sages name different trees (willow, olive, oleander/hardufni etc.); one opinion that the bitter tree healed bitter water; and a reading of 'tree' as words of Torah. Confirm the section and opinions.
'A song that Jews still sing every morning': the Song at the Sea (Az Yashir) in Pesukei de-Zimra; confirm.

Editor review: Proverbs 3:18 calls wisdom a tree of life, not the words of Torah; now says the rabbis link the two. Cut 'every morning' and the stock 'carried far beyond the wilderness'; howItsDone no longer puts a modern-wording quotation in quote marks.
